ukmt-jmc-2015-01.title: Look at what is subtracted
ukmt-jmc-2015-01.body:
All five use the numbers $1,2,3,4$, so the largest answer is the one where the least is subtracted. A subtracts only $2$; B subtracts $3$; C subtracts $4$; D subtracts $3$ and $4$; E subtracts $2$ and $3$. So A is largest.

**Answer: (A) $1-2+3+4$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-02.title: Count up to the hour
ukmt-jmc-2015-02.body:
From 22:22 to 23:00 is $60-22=38$ minutes. From 23:00 to midnight is another $60$ minutes. Total $38+60=98$ minutes.

**Answer: (E) 98**

ukmt-jmc-2015-02.title: Subtract from 24:00
ukmt-jmc-2015-02.body:
Midnight is 24:00. From 22:22 to 24:00 is $1$ hour $38$ minutes, i.e. $60+38=98$ minutes.

**Answer: (E) 98**

ukmt-jmc-2015-03.title: Eliminate options
ukmt-jmc-2015-03.body:
$12\,345$ and $15$ are both odd, so the answer is odd: only A, D, E remain. The answer is clearly much bigger than $1$ and much smaller than $12\,345$, so it must be $823$ (check: $823\times15 = 12\,345$).

**Answer: (D) 823**

ukmt-jmc-2015-04.title: Work down the pyramid
ukmt-jmc-2015-04.body:
Each number is the sum of the two below it, so work downwards by subtracting.

- Second row: the box next to $47$ is $105-47=58$.
- Third row: $58 = 31 + q$, so the middle box is $q=27$; then $47 = 27 + r$ gives $r=20$.
- Fourth row: $20 = 13 + s$, so $s=7$.
- Bottom row: $13 = 9 + t$, so the box next to $9$ is $t=4$; finally $s = t + x$, so $7 = 4 + x$ and $x=3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2015-05.title: Subtract the fractions
ukmt-jmc-2015-05.body:
$\frac13-\frac14=\frac{4-3}{12}=\frac1{12}$. So $\frac1{12}$ of the number is $3$, and the number is $12\times 3=36$.

**Answer: (B) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2015-06.title: Exterior angle
ukmt-jmc-2015-06.body:
The angle inside the triangle at the top vertex is on a straight line with the $110^\circ$ angle, so it is $180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ$. The $120^\circ$ angle is an exterior angle of the triangle, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $120 = x + 70$, giving $x=50$.

**Answer: (B) 50**

ukmt-jmc-2015-06.title: Angle sum
ukmt-jmc-2015-06.body:
Interior angles: top $=180-110=70$, bottom right $=180-120=60$. So $x = 180-70-60 = 50$.

**Answer: (B) 50**

ukmt-jmc-2015-07.title: Look at the last digit
ukmt-jmc-2015-07.body:
$9\times8=72$, so the product ends in $2$, not $1$. To change $987\,654\,321$ into a number ending in $2$, the digits $1$ and $2$ must be swapped. Their sum is $1+2=3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2015-08.title: Use oddness
ukmt-jmc-2015-08.body:
All the options are odd, so each leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $2$. We need remainder $1$ on division by $3$ as well: $3\to0$, $5\to2$, $7\to1$, $9\to0$, $11\to2$. Only $7$ works.

**Answer: (C) 7**

ukmt-jmc-2015-09.title: Estimate
ukmt-jmc-2015-09.body:
He has had the machine for $63-50=13$ years. $25\,048\div13\approx 26\,000\div 13 = 2000$ miles per year.

**Answer: (D) 2000**

ukmt-jmc-2015-10.title: Multiply when it helps
ukmt-jmc-2015-10.body:
Multiplying two whole numbers bigger than 1 gives at least as much as adding them, but multiplying by $1$ wastes the $1$. So add the $1$ and multiply the rest: $1+2\times3\times4 = 1+24 = 25$.

**Answer: (E) 25**

ukmt-jmc-2015-10.title: Try all 8 choices
ukmt-jmc-2015-10.body:
There are only $2^3=8$ ways to fill the boxes. Remembering to multiply before adding: $+++$ gives $10$, $++\times$ gives $15$, $+\times+$ gives $11$, $+\times\times$ gives $25$, $\times++$ gives $9$, $\times+\times$ gives $14$, $\times\times+$ gives $10$, $\times\times\times$ gives $24$. The largest is $25$.

**Answer: (E) 25**

ukmt-jmc-2015-11.title: Avoid the prime 2
ukmt-jmc-2015-11.body:
If one of the three primes is $2$, the other two are odd, so the sum is even and bigger than $2$, hence not prime. So use three odd primes. $3+5+7=15$ is not prime. Next smallest: $3+5+11=19$, which is prime. Any other triple of odd primes has a larger sum ($3+7+11=21$, $5+7+11=23$, ...).

**Answer: (D) 19**

ukmt-jmc-2015-11.title: Check the options
ukmt-jmc-2015-11.body:
$11$ and $17$: sums of three different odd primes start at $15$, then $19$; and a sum including $2$ is even. $15$ is not prime. $19 = 3+5+11$ works, and it is the smallest option that does.

**Answer: (D) 19**

ukmt-jmc-2015-12.title: Think in thirds
ukmt-jmc-2015-12.body:
The fish is $2$ kg plus one third of itself, so the $2$ kg must be the other two thirds. Two thirds $=2$ kg means one third $=1$ kg, so the whole fish is $3$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2015-12.title: Equation
ukmt-jmc-2015-12.body:
Let the weight be $w$. Then $w = 2 + \frac13 w$, so $\frac23 w = 2$ and $w = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2015-13.title: List the multiples of 3
ukmt-jmc-2015-13.body:
Every pair of the numbers $1$ to $8$ is joined by a line, so we count pairs with sum a multiple of $3$ (sums go up to $15$):

- $3$: $1+2$
- $6$: $1+5,\ 2+4$
- $9$: $1+8,\ 2+7,\ 3+6,\ 4+5$
- $12$: $4+8,\ 5+7$
- $15$: $7+8$

Total $1+2+4+2+1=10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

ukmt-jmc-2015-13.title: Use remainders
ukmt-jmc-2015-13.body:
Sort $1,\dots,8$ by remainder on division by 3: remainder 0: $\{3,6\}$; remainder 1: $\{1,4,7\}$; remainder 2: $\{2,5,8\}$. A sum is a multiple of 3 if both numbers have remainder 0 ($1$ pair) or one has remainder 1 and the other remainder 2 ($3\times3=9$ pairs). Total $10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

ukmt-jmc-2015-14.title: Check each prime digit
ukmt-jmc-2015-14.body:
The prime digits are $2, 3, 5, 7$ (remember $1$ is not prime). Counting bars in the diagram: $2$ uses $5$ bars, $3$ uses $5$, $5$ uses $5$, and $7$ uses $3$. All of $5,5,5,3$ are prime, so all four digits work.

**Answer: (E) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2015-15.title: Rule out with primes
ukmt-jmc-2015-15.body:
A prime divides a product only if it divides one of the factors.

- A: neither $23$ nor $34$ is a multiple of $3$.
- B: neither $34$ nor $45$ is a multiple of $7$.
- D and E: neither factor is a multiple of $5$.

So only C can work.

**Answer: (C) $45\times56$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-15.title: Check C directly
ukmt-jmc-2015-15.body:
$45 = 9\times5$ and $56 = 8\times7$, so $45\times56 = 8\times9\times5\times7 = 2520$, which is the lowest common multiple of $1,2,\dots,10$. So it is divisible by all of them.

**Answer: (C) $45\times56$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-16.title: Angle sums
ukmt-jmc-2015-16.body:
Let the bottom corner of the square be $R$, and let the angles at $R$ between the base and the square's sides be $p^\circ$ (left) and $q^\circ$ (right). The angles on the base at $R$ give $p+90+q=180$, so $p+q=90$.

In the left small triangle the angles are $x$, $p$ and $60$, so $x+p=120$. Similarly $y+q=120$. Adding: $x+y = 240-(p+q) = 240-90=150$.

**Answer: (D) 150**

ukmt-jmc-2015-16.title: Special case check
ukmt-jmc-2015-16.body:
The answer can't depend on how the square is tilted, so suppose it is symmetric: $p=q=45$. Then $x = 180-60-45 = 75$ and likewise $y=75$, so $x+y=150$. (This is a quick check; the first method shows it holds in general.)

**Answer: (D) 150**

ukmt-jmc-2015-17.title: Two cases
ukmt-jmc-2015-17.body:
If Hearts is telling the truth, then Clubs lies, so Diamonds tells the truth, so Spades lies: 2 truthful.

If Hearts is lying, then Clubs tells the truth, Diamonds lies, Spades tells the truth: again 2 truthful.

We can't tell who stole the tarts, but either way exactly 2 Knaves tell the truth.

**Answer: (B) 2**

ukmt-jmc-2015-17.title: Alternating pattern
ukmt-jmc-2015-17.body:
Each Knave after the first says the previous one is lying, so truth and lies must alternate along the chain Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds, Spades: T, L, T, L or L, T, L, T. Either way, 2 of the 4 are truthful.

**Answer: (B) 2**

ukmt-jmc-2015-18.title: Spot the doubling
ukmt-jmc-2015-18.body:
$5274 = 2\times 2637$ and $36\,918 = 2\times18\,459$. So the second fraction equals the first one with top and bottom doubled, and it also simplifies to $\frac17$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac17$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-19.title: Check the cubes in order
ukmt-jmc-2015-19.body:
The cubes are $1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, \dots$.

- $27, 64$: three cubes smaller than $27$ come from $1, 8$ and sum to at most $24$; for $64$ the parts would come from $1, 8, 27$, and no three of these add to $64$ (the largest is $81$, and $27+27+8=62$, $27+27+1=55$).
- $125$: since $3\times27=81<125$, one cube must be $64$ (two $64$s are too much), leaving $61$ from two of $1,8,27$ — impossible.
- $216 = 27+64+125$. ✓

**Answer: (D) 216**

ukmt-jmc-2015-19.title: Search directly
ukmt-jmc-2015-19.body:
Trying all sums $a^3+b^3+c^3$ with $1\le a\le b\le c\le 5$ and looking for a cube, the first hit is $3^3+4^3+5^3 = 27+64+125=216=6^3$.

**Answer: (D) 216**

ukmt-jmc-2015-20.title: Look from six directions
ukmt-jmc-2015-20.body:
The layers are $4\times4$, $3\times3$, $2\times2$ and $1\times1$ ($16+9+4+1=30$ cubes).

- From below you see the $4\times4$ base: $16\,\text{m}^2$.
- From above you also see exactly a $4\times4$ square's worth of top faces: $16\,\text{m}^2$.
- From each of the four sides you see a staircase of $4+3+2+1=10$ squares: $10\,\text{m}^2$, and every side face is visible from exactly one side.

Total $16+16+4\times10 = 72\,\text{m}^2$.

**Answer: (C) $72\,\text{m}^2$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-20.title: Layer by layer
ukmt-jmc-2015-20.body:
Each layer's vertical sides: a $k\times k$ layer has $4k$ side faces, giving $4(4+3+2+1)=40$. Horizontal faces: the bottom $16$, plus the top faces, which in total cover the same $4\times4$ area seen from above: $16$. Total $40+16+16=72$.

**Answer: (C) $72\,\text{m}^2$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-21.title: Find the gap
ukmt-jmc-2015-21.body:
Let each of the three gaps be $g$ mm. Then $4\times420+3g=4800$, so $3g=3120$ and $g=1040$. The two middle pictures are separated by one gap, which is centred on the centre line. The centre of each middle picture is half a gap plus half a picture from the centre line: $520+210 = 730$ mm.

**Answer: (C) 730 mm**

ukmt-jmc-2015-21.title: Use the centres
ukmt-jmc-2015-21.body:
The outer pictures' centres are $210$ mm from each end, so they are $4800-420=4380$ mm apart. Equal spacing of identical pictures means equally spaced centres, so consecutive centres are $4380\div3=1460$ mm apart. The middle two centres are $1460$ mm apart, symmetric about the centre line, so each is $730$ mm from it.

**Answer: (C) 730 mm**

ukmt-jmc-2015-22.title: Complete the grid and use symmetry
ukmt-jmc-2015-22.body:
Extend the lines of the small equilateral triangles across the whole hexagon. The hexagon is then made of small equilateral triangles, plus half-triangles along its edges. By symmetry it is enough to look at one sixth of the hexagon (the part between the centre and one edge). In that sixth there are $6$ shaded small triangles, and the unshaded part is $4$ whole small triangles plus $4$ half triangles, i.e. $6$ small triangles' worth. So shaded and unshaded areas are equal.

**Answer: (E) $\frac12$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-23.title: Find the rectangle, then compare areas
ukmt-jmc-2015-23.body:
The squares have sides $1, 2, 3, 4$ cm. The white region lies above the $1\times1$ square in the bottom-left corner and below the $3\times3$ square in the top-left corner, so it has width $1$ cm; its area is $1.5$, so its height is $1.5$ cm. The left side of the rectangle is therefore $3+1.5+1 = 5.5$ cm, and the bottom is $1+4=5$ cm, so the rectangle has area $27.5\,\text{cm}^2$.

The squares cover $27.5-1.5 = 26\,\text{cm}^2$, but their areas add to $1+4+9+16=30\,\text{cm}^2$. The extra $30-26=4\,\text{cm}^2$ is counted twice, i.e. it is the overlap.

**Answer: (D) $4\,\text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-23.title: Measure the overlaps
ukmt-jmc-2015-23.body:
With the rectangle $5$ wide and $5.5$ tall: the $4\times4$ square (bottom right) reaches up to height $4$, and the $3\times3$ square (top left) reaches down to height $2.5$ and across to $x=3$; the $4\times4$ square starts at $x=1$. Their overlap is $2$ wide and $4-2.5=1.5$ tall: $3\,\text{cm}^2$. The $2\times2$ square (top right) spans $x\in[3,5]$ and heights $[3.5,5.5]$, so it overlaps the big square in a $2\times0.5$ strip: $1\,\text{cm}^2$. Total $4\,\text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (D) $4\,\text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-24.title: Divisibility by 5 and 9
ukmt-jmc-2015-24.body:
Write the palindrome as $abcba$. It must be a multiple of $5$ and of $9$. A multiple of $5$ ends in $0$ or $5$; it can't end in $0$ (then it would start with $0$), so $a=5$: the number is $5bcb5$, with digit sum $10+2b+c$, which must be a multiple of $9$.

- Smallest: take $b=0$; $10+c$ is a multiple of 9 when $c=8$: $50805$.
- Largest: take $b=9$; $28+c$ is a multiple of 9 when $c=8$: $59895$.

Difference: $59895-50805 = 9090$.

**Answer: (B) 9090**

ukmt-jmc-2015-24.title: Shortcut for the difference
ukmt-jmc-2015-24.body:
Both numbers have the form $5b8b5$, so their difference comes only from the $b$ digits in the thousands and tens places: $(9-0)\times1010 = 9090$.

**Answer: (B) 9090**

ukmt-jmc-2015-25.title: Isosceles triangle and exterior angles
ukmt-jmc-2015-25.body:
Since $VU=VW$, triangle $VUW$ is isosceles, so $\angle VUW=\angle VWU$; call this $t^\circ$. Also $\angle YWX = \angle VWU = t^\circ$ (vertically opposite).

- In triangle $UZX$, $\angle VUW$ (that is, $\angle VUX$) is an exterior angle, so $t = z + x$.
- In triangle $WYX$, $\angle VYZ$ is an exterior angle, so $y = t + x$.

Substituting: $y = z + 2x$, so $x = \frac{y-z}{2}$.

**Answer: (E) $x=\frac{y-z}{2}$**

ukmt-jmc-2015-25.title: Angle sum in the big triangle
ukmt-jmc-2015-25.body:
With $t$ as before, the angle of triangle $VUW$ at $V$ is $180-2t$. Triangle $ZYV$ has angles $z$ at $Z$, $y$ at $Y$ and $180-2t$ at $V$, so $z+y+180-2t=180$, i.e. $2t=y+z$. From triangle $UZX$, $t=z+x$. Hence $2z+2x=y+z$, so $x=\frac{y-z}{2}$.

**Answer: (E) $x=\frac{y-z}{2}$**
